title: The rule of law
body: The rule of law means everyone, including the government, is bound by clear public laws applied equally by independent courts. It is what lets people and businesses plan, invest and challenge abuse of power. Without it, outcomes depend on who you know.

title: Criminal law versus civil law
body: Criminal law deals with wrongs against society: the state prosecutes, and punishment can include prison. Civil law settles disputes between people or companies, such as contracts, debts, property and family matters: the claimant sues, usually for money or a court order.

title: Standards of proof
body: In a criminal trial, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, because liberty is at stake. In a civil case, the claimant wins on a balance of probabilities: more likely than not. That is why someone can be acquitted of a crime yet lose a civil claim.

title: Zimbabwe's Roman-Dutch roots
body: Zimbabwe's common law is Roman-Dutch law, brought via the Cape Colony, shaped by English law in procedure and commerce. Customary law also applies in areas like family and inheritance. Above all of these sits the Constitution.

title: The 2013 Constitution
body: Zimbabwe's current Constitution was approved in a referendum in March 2013 and came into force that year. It is the supreme law: any law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid. Its Declaration of Rights protects freedoms such as expression, assembly and a fair trial.

title: Separation of powers
body: Power is split between the legislature (makes laws), the executive (runs government) and the judiciary (interprets laws and settles disputes). Each checks the others: courts can strike down unconstitutional laws, and parliament controls the budget.

title: What makes a valid contract
body: A contract needs agreement (offer and acceptance), an intention to be legally bound, parties with capacity, a lawful and possible purpose, and any required formalities. Unlike English law, Roman-Dutch law as used in Zimbabwe and South Africa does not require 'consideration'.

title: When a contract is broken
body: If a party breaches a contract, the other can usually claim damages to be put where they would have been had it been performed. In Roman-Dutch law they may also demand specific performance, or cancel if the breach is serious enough.

title: Delict: the law of wrongs
body: A delict (called a tort in English law) is a wrongful act that causes harm and gives the victim a claim for compensation, such as a car crash through careless driving or defamation. Typical elements: conduct, wrongfulness, fault, causation and harm.

title: Negligence and the reasonable person
body: You are negligent if you fall below the care a reasonable person would take in your position and it was foreseeable that someone could be harmed. Professionals such as engineers and doctors are judged against a reasonable member of their profession.

title: Innocent until proven guilty
body: The presumption of innocence means the state must prove guilt; the accused does not have to prove innocence. It is protected in Zimbabwe's Constitution and in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Suspects are not criminals until a court convicts them.

title: Your rights on arrest
body: Under section 50 of Zimbabwe's Constitution, an arrested person must be told why, may remain silent, may contact a lawyer and a relative, and must be brought before a court within 48 hours. Confessions obtained by force cannot be used.

title: Guilty act, guilty mind
body: Most crimes need two parts: actus reus, the prohibited act, and mens rea, the guilty state of mind such as intention or recklessness. Accidentally taking someone's identical bag is not theft, because the intention to steal is missing.

title: Types of intellectual property
body: Patents protect inventions; copyright protects creative works like code, music and books; trademarks protect brand names and logos; trade secrets protect confidential know-how such as recipes. Each has different rules, costs and durations.

title: Copyright is automatic
body: Copyright arises automatically when an original work is recorded, with no registration needed in most countries. It protects the expression, not the idea: you can write your own app with the same features, but not copy someone's code. It typically lasts decades after the author's death.

title: Patents: a deal with society
body: A patent gives an inventor the exclusive right to an invention, usually for 20 years from filing. In exchange, the invention is published so others can learn from it. It must be new, inventive and useful, and filing publicly before applying can destroy novelty.

title: A company is a legal person
body: A registered company is a separate legal person: it owns assets, signs contracts and can sue and be sued. Shareholders' liability is limited to what they invested. The classic case is Salomon v Salomon (1897), but courts can 'pierce the veil' in cases of fraud.
source_name: Wikipedia: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd

title: Employment law basics
body: Employment law balances bargaining power between employers and workers: written terms, minimum standards for hours and leave, fair dismissal procedures and safe workplaces. In Zimbabwe the main statute is the Labour Act, and disputes can go to the Labour Court.

title: Data protection
body: Data protection laws control how organisations collect and use personal data: a lawful reason, only what is needed, kept secure, and rights for people to see and correct their data. The EU's GDPR is the best-known model; Zimbabwe passed its Cyber and Data Protection Act in 2021.

title: Precedent
body: Under the doctrine of precedent (stare decisis), lower courts follow the legal reasoning of higher courts in similar cases. It makes law predictable. Only the reasoning essential to the decision (the ratio decidendi) binds; side remarks (obiter dicta) merely persuade.

title: Statutes and common law
body: Statutes are written laws passed by parliament. Common law is law developed by courts through cases. When they conflict, a valid statute wins over common law, and the Constitution wins over both. Lawyers always check for the latest amendments.

title: Customary law
body: Customary law is the traditional law of communities, shaped by practice rather than written statutes. Zimbabwe's Constitution recognises it, especially in family, inheritance and land matters, but customs that conflict with constitutional rights such as equality are invalid.

title: The Universal Declaration
body: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948. It is not itself a binding treaty, but it inspired binding treaties and many national constitutions, and some of its rights are now seen as customary international law.
source_name: Wikipedia: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

title: How international law binds
body: International law comes mainly from treaties that states agree to and from customary law built on consistent state practice. There is no world police: enforcement relies on courts like the ICJ, sanctions, reciprocity and reputation.

title: Lawyer-client privilege
body: Confidential communications between a client and lawyer for legal advice are generally protected from disclosure, even to courts. It exists so people can speak frankly to their lawyers. It does not cover advice sought to commit a crime or fraud.

title: Due diligence
body: Before an investment or acquisition, buyers and investors run due diligence: checking company registration, contracts, debts, intellectual property ownership, tax, licences and legal disputes. Startups that keep clean records get funded faster.

title: Proof in criminal trials
body: Legal procedure check.
statement: Criminal cases are decided on a balance of probabilities
explanation: Criminal guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. The balance of probabilities is the civil standard.

title: Verbal agreements
body: Contract check.
statement: A contract must be in writing to be valid
explanation: Most contracts are valid when made orally, though some, such as sales of land, must be in writing. Writing mainly helps prove the terms.

title: The 48-hour rule
body: Rights check.
statement: In Zimbabwe, a person arrested must be taken to court within 48 hours
explanation: Section 50 of the Constitution requires an arrested person to be brought before a court within 48 hours.

title: Shareholder liability
body: Company law check.
statement: Shareholders are personally liable for all of a limited company's debts
explanation: Shareholders normally risk only what they invested. The company is a separate legal person responsible for its own debts.

title: How long patents last
body: IP check.
statement: A patent usually lasts 20 years from filing
explanation: Most countries follow the TRIPS minimum of 20 years from the filing date, provided renewal fees are paid.
